lit.'<p><b>Oxidación = pérdida de electrones:
'

Oxidation = loss of electrons. Zn gives up its 2 e⁻: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2 e⁻. Its oxidation number increases from 0 to +2 and the atom shrinks as it becomes a cation. Today it is defined by electrons, not by oxygen: Zn is oxidized even though there is no O₂ here.

'
lit.'<p><b>Reducción = ganancia de electrone:
'

Reduction = gain of electrons. Cu²⁺ receives those 2 e⁻: Cu²⁺ + 2 e⁻ → Cu. Its oxidation number decreases from +2 to 0 and the ion becomes a metallic copper atom, larger than the ion.

'
lit.'<p>El <b>número de oxidación</b> es la:
'

The oxidation number is the charge an atom would have if the electrons were assigned to the more electronegative element. Here there is a metallic Zn atom (oxidation number 0) next to a Cu²⁺ ion (+2). The yellow spheres are the 2 e⁻ that will change owner in Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu.

'
lit.'<p>La especie que <b>se oxida</b> cede:
'

The species that is oxidized gives up electrons and therefore causes the other to be reduced: it is the reducing agent (orange ring). The one that is reduced takes them up and causes the other to be oxidized: it is the oxidizing agent (blue ring). See it in three cases: Zn + Cu²⁺, Na + Cl₂ and Cl₂ + Br⁻.

'
lit.'<p>Ninguna de las dos semirreacciones o:
'

Neither half-reaction happens alone: the electrons one species loses are exactly those the other gains (here, 2 e⁻). Adding them gives the overall reaction Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, and the sum of the oxidation numbers (+2) is conserved.

'
